statement: A UC Berkeley study found California's $20 fast-food wage raised average weekly wages for covered workers by about 11 percent without reducing employment, and raised prices by 1.5 percent (6 cents on a $4 item), with employers passing about 50 percent of higher costs to consumers.

increased average weekly wages for covered fast food workers by about 11 percent and did not reduce employment. Compared to controls, prices increased by 1.5 percent, equivalent to 6 cents for a $4 item. Employers passed about 50 percent of the higher wage costs to consumers
context: Working paper by Sosinskiy and Reich, UC Berkeley Center on Wage and Employment Dynamics, 2026-04-01; not peer reviewed; the center's director has long supported higher minimum wages. statement: Dube's 2019 review for the UK government concluded that research from the US, UK and other developed countries points to a very muted effect of minimum wages on employment, and that there is room for a National Living Wage of 60% to two-thirds of median hourly earnings.
anchor: Overall the most up to date body of research from US, UK and other developed countries points to a very muted effect of minimum wages on employment, while significantly increasing the earnings of low paid workers.
there is room for exploring a more ambitious NLW remit in the UK in the coming years, in the range of 60% to two-thirds of median hourly earnings.
context: Independent review by Arindrajit Dube (UMass Amherst) commissioned by HM Treasury and BEIS, published 4 November 2019 under the Open Government Licence; not peer reviewed. A literature review plus new analysis of seven high-minimum-wage US states and the UK National Living Wage; the author has published widely finding small employment effects, and the review itself says the evidence on high minimum wages is still developing. Written for the Conservative government's remit decision, which is relevant to the US two-thirds-of-median target.

statement: Dube's review found US state evidence suggests employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage, that county-level evidence held at up to 81% of the median, and that in the 7 highest-wage US states, where the minimum binds for around 17% of the workforce, effects were similarly modest.
anchor: Across US states, the best evidence suggests that the employment effects are small up to around 59% of the median wage. Evidence using sub-state county-level variation found this to hold even in lower wage counties where the minimum stood at up to 81% of the median wage.
in the 7 US states with the highest minimum wage, where the minimum is binding for around 17% of the workforce, employment effects have been similarly modest.
context: HM Treasury and BEIS commissioned review by Arindrajit Dube, November 2019; not peer reviewed. The 59% and 81% figures summarize studies by Dube and co-authors (the 81% county result is Godøy and Reich); the seven-state result is new analysis in Technical Annex A. A two-thirds of median floor would sit above 59% and below 81%, so the review's own evidence for that range rests on the county studies and the seven-state analysis.

statement: Dustmann and co-authors found that Germany's new national minimum wage, which affected 15% of employees, raised wages without lowering employment, moved low-wage workers to larger, higher-paying and more productive establishments, and accounted for up to 17% of the wage increase through that upgrading.

we find that the minimum wage raised wages but did
not lower employment. It also led to the reallocation of low-wage workers from
smaller to larger, from lower- to higher-paying, and from less to more productive
establishments. This worker upgrading accounts for up to 17% of the wage increase induced by the minimum wage.
context: Quarterly Journal of Economics 137(1), 2022, peer reviewed, open access (CC BY 4.0); authors at Germany's Institute for Employment Research (IAB) using administrative data, individual and regional designs. The paper's setting is a floor near half of median earnings (EV-WRK-057), below a two-thirds target, and short-run (to 2018).

statement: Bossler and Gerner found that Germany's new statutory minimum wage, implemented on January 1, 2015, raised average wages 3.8% to 6.3% and cut employment about 1.7% in affected establishments, implying a labor demand elasticity between −0.2 and −0.4.
anchor: The authors present the first evidence on the consequences of the new statutory minimum wage in Germany, which was implemented on January 1, 2015.

A difference-in-differences estimation reveals an increase in average wages between 3.8% and 6.3% and an employment loss by approximately 1.7% in establishments affected by the minimum wage. These estimates imply a labor demand elasticity with respect to wages ranging between −0.2 and −0.4.
context: ILR Review 73(5), 2020, peer reviewed; establishment-level difference-in-differences using the IAB Establishment Panel, short run to 2015. Contests Dustmann and co-authors on employment: it finds a reduction in hires concentrated in affected establishments, a transitory reduction in hours, and notes effects may be larger in a downturn. The authors are at IAB-linked institutes; the two German studies use different data and units (establishments versus workers and regions).

statement: Jardim and co-authors found that Seattle's second increase, to $13 in 2016, cut hours worked in low-wage jobs by 6-7 percent while hourly wages rose 3 percent, lowering pay by an average of $74 a month per job, while restaurant employment at all wage levels showed an effect of zero.
anchor: we conclude that the second wage increase to $13 reduced hours worked in low-wage jobs by 6-7 percent, while hourly wages in such jobs increased by 3 percent. Consequently, total payroll for such jobs decreased, implying that the Ordinance lowered the amount paid to workers in low-wage jobs by an average of $74 per month per job in 2016.
We estimate an effect of zero when analyzing employment in the restaurant industry at all wage levels, comparable to many prior studies.
context: NBER Working Paper 23532 (June 2017, revised May 2018) by University of Washington researchers (Seattle Minimum Wage Study, funded by the City of Seattle); this is a working paper, and a later journal version may give different estimates (the revision already lowered the monthly loss figure). Washington administrative payroll and hours data allow all low-wage jobs, not only restaurants, to be tracked, but the sample over-represents smaller single-site employers, and the authors note effects may be non-linear and local rather than general.

statement: Reich, Allegretto and Godøy found Seattle's minimum wage up to $13 raised food-service wages without a detectable employment effect, even among limited-service restaurants, while noting Seattle's hot labor market may have raised employment.
anchor: Employment in food service, however, was not affected, even among the limited-service restaurants, many of them franchisees, for whom the policy was most binding. These findings extend our knowledge of minimum wage effects to policies as high as $13.

Of course, unobserved factors, such as Seattle’s hot labor market compared to that in Synthetic Seattle (Tu, Lerman and Gates 2017), may have positively affected Seattle’s low-wage employment during this period.
context: UC Berkeley Center on Wage and Employment Dynamics brief, June 2017, not peer reviewed; synthetic-control method on county and city payroll counts (QCEW), covering the food services industry only, which the authors use as a proxy for low-wage work. Contests the University of Washington finding (EV-WRK-060), which covers all low-wage jobs and hours; critics note restaurants include workers above the wage floor and the tip credit softened the wage increase.

statement: Seattle's first phase in April 2015 raised the minimum from $9.47 to $10 or $11 depending on business size, tipped workers and health insurance, and its second phase from January 1, 2016 set four levels from $10.50 to $13 depending on employer size.

statement: Godøy and Reich found positive wage effects and no detectable adverse effects on employment, weekly hours or weeks worked in low-wage counties with relative minimum wage ratios as high as 0.82, and substantial declines in household and child poverty in high-impact counties.
anchor: In this article, we examine minimum wage effects in low-wage counties, where relative minimum wage ratios reach as high as 0.82, well beyond the state-based ratios in extant studies.
We find positive wage effects, especially in high-impact counties, but do not detect adverse effects on employment, weekly hours, or annual weeks worked.
In high-impact counties, we find substantial declines in household and child poverty.
context: Industrial Relations 60(1), 2021, peer reviewed; event-study and difference-in-differences designs on ACS, QWI and QCEW data, by UC Berkeley researchers whose group has long found small employment effects. Written to inform whether a $15 federal minimum should exempt low-wage areas; the ratios refer to minimum to county median, and results rest on the federal and state increases of 2000 to 2016, not on current $15-plus floors in every county.

statement: Clemens and Wither found that the 2007 to 2009 federal minimum wage increases had significant negative effects on the employment and income growth of targeted low-skilled workers in states fully bound by them, reducing aggregate employment rates there by at least half of a percentage point.

we find that binding minimum wage increases had significant, negative effects on the employment and income growth of targeted workers.
reduced aggregate employment rates by at least half of a percentage point in states that were bound by the federal minimum wage increases.
context: Journal of Public Economics 170, 2019, peer reviewed; authors at UC San Diego and the Federal Reserve, Clemens is a frequent critic of large increases. Uses the 2008 SIPP panel and treats the Great Recession as the setting, so it bears on a recession off-ramp; the authors acknowledge important limitations in their research designs and that their estimates are large relative to past research.

statement: Renkin, Montialoux and Siegenthaler found that a 10% minimum wage hike raises grocery prices by 0.36%, consistent with full pass-through of cost increases, with prices rising equally for goods bought by low-income and high-income households.
anchor: We find that a 10% minimum wage hike translates into a 0.36% increase in the prices of grocery products. This magnitude is consistent with a full pass-through of cost increases into consumer prices.
Prices rise to the same extent for goods consumed by low-income and high-income households.
Our results suggest that consumers rather than firms bear the cost of minimum wage increases in the retail sector.
context: Review of Economics and Statistics, 2020, peer reviewed; supermarket scanner data across many state increases, 2001 to 2012. Covers grocery and drug stores, not restaurants or services, and state-level increases much smaller than a move to two-thirds of median; effects at larger increases and in labor-intensive sectors may differ.

statement: Dube found that the long-run elasticity of the non-elderly poverty rate with respect to the minimum wage ranges between −0.220 and −0.459, with income gains from tax credits and transfers about 66 percent as large after a reduction in public assistance.

context: American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 11(4), 2019, peer reviewed; CPS-based state panel by a UMass Amherst economist who also wrote the HM Treasury review (EV-WRK-050), so the two are not independent. statement: Neumark and Yen found that higher tipped minimum wages (smaller tip credits) reduce jobs among tipped restaurant workers without earnings gains large enough to raise total earnings, with an employment elasticity around −.08.

We find evidence of negative effects on employment, with employment elasticities around −.08.
context: NBER Working Paper 29213 (September 2021, revised August 2022), by UC Irvine economists long critical of large increases; a working paper using past state variation in tip credits. The Employment Policies Institute, a restaurant-industry funded group, has promoted this paper in its own summaries, which frame the elasticity as up to a 6.1% employment loss per dollar; those summaries were not read as sources here. Cross-state variation in tip credits was mostly modest, so the design says little about full elimination.

statement: Neumark and Yen found most of their evidence gave no indication that higher tipped minimum wages would be well targeted to poor or low-income families or reduce the likelihood of being poor or very low income.

In July 2025, the Council adopted an act that changes Initiative 82 to freeze the minimum wage for tipped workers at $10/hour until July 1, 2026, then gradually increases those wages to 75% of the standard minimum wage by 2034.
locator: Summary statement of Referendum Measure No. 009
context: District of Columbia Board of Elections notice, 22 October 2025, formulating a referendum on the Council's act; a notice from the elections authority, neutral on merits. A referendum on the act was proposed in October 2025; the outcome and any change since was not confirmed in this research (a new Initiative 87 to end the tipped wage was reported in November 2026 as having delivered petition signatures). Re-check DC law before use.

statement: Chicago's City Council approved the One Fair Wage ordinance in October 2023, phasing out the tipped subminimum wage over five years, with the $9.48 tipped wage rising 8 percent a year to reach parity with the $15.80 standard minimum wage.
anchor: the City Council approved the One Fair Wage ordinance, a proposal to phase out the City’s subminimum wage for tipped workers over a five-year period.
earn a subminimum wage of $9.48 per hour to increase by 8 percent per year until it reaches parity with Chicago’s standard hourly minimum wage of $15.80.
context: City of Chicago Mayor's Press Office, 6 October 2023, an announcement by the administration that backed the ordinance, not the ordinance text. A compromise with the Illinois Restaurant Association stretched the phase-out from two to five years; the ordinance should be cited directly for the dates and the 2028 end point. No outcome data were found.

statement: GAO reported that, as of 2023, fewer than half of the roughly 1,000 former 14(c) workers Colorado and Oregon could track had moved to other employment, and 54 to 61 percent were not working but received Medicaid-funded non-employment services.
anchor: GAO’s analysis of data from two selected states that
eliminated the use of 14(c) certificates—Colorado and Oregon—provides a partial
picture of outcomes in those states.
As of 2023 (the most recent data
available), fewer than half of the approximately 1,000 people these states were
able to track had moved from 14(c) to some other type of employment.
The remaining 54 to 61 percent of people the states were able to track were not
working but were receiving non-employment services funded by Medicaid, such as
day services to build socialization and daily living skills.
context: Government Accountability Office, nonpartisan legislative-branch agency, report GAO-25-106471, April 2025. Partial picture: both states track people mainly through Medicaid records and could not follow those who left Medicaid; Oregon's data cover people with intellectual and developmental disabilities, not all 14(c) workers. The report notes untracked individuals may be working, retired, ineligible or deceased.

statement: Kakara, Bair and Venkataramani found that repealing Section 14(c) in New Hampshire (2015) was followed by a 5.2 percentage point rise in labor force participation and 7 points in employment for people with cognitive disabilities, while Maryland's (2016) changes were not statistically significant.
anchor: Repeal of Section 14(c) in New Hampshire (2015) and Maryland (2016).

In state-specific analyses, New Hampshire’s labor force participation and employment had a statistically significant increase by 5.2 percentage points (β = 0.05; 95% CI, 0-0.10; P = .04) and 7 percentage points (β = 0.07; 95% CI, 0.01-0.13; P = .03), respectively, following Section 14(c) repeal.
Labor force participation and employment both increased in Maryland, although estimates were not statistically significant.
context: JAMA Health Forum, 2024, peer reviewed; synthetic difference-in-differences on ACS 2010 to 2019 for ages 18 to 45 with a cognitive disability, two states only, by University of Pennsylvania researchers. The authors note New Hampshire had no 14(c) workers at repeal and that Maryland phased out over four years, so the effects may reflect state funding and signaling rather than wage floors; hours and wages for the employed did not change significantly.

statement: The U.S. Commission on Civil Rights majority recommended in 2020 that Congress repeal Section 14(c) with a planned phase-out period and expand funding for supported employment, prioritizing capacity building in states transitioning from 14(c).
anchor: Congress should repeal Section 14(c) with a planned phase-out period to allow transition
among service providers and people with disabilities to alternative service models prioritizing
competitive integrated employment.
Congress should expand funding for supported employment services and prioritize capacity
building in states transitioning from 14(c) programs.
locator: Statement of the Chair and highlighted recommendations
context: U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, independent bipartisan federal commission, September 2020 (first Trump administration period); a majority report with separate statements, so it is a recommendation of the commission majority, not a finding of causal effects. It drew on testimony, two field visits and public comments both for and against the program; it recommended continued outcome data collection after phase-out.

statement: DiNardo and Lee (2004) compared employers where unions barely won or barely lost elections in 1984-1999 and found small impacts of unionization on business survival, employment, output, productivity and wages, with wage estimates close to zero.
anchor: Essentially, outcomes for employers where unions barely won the election (e.g., by one vote) are compared with those where the unions barely lost.
The analysis finds small impacts on all outcomes that we examine; estimates for wages are close to zero.
establishments that faced organizing drives in the United States during 1984–1999
context: Quarterly Journal of Economics, peer reviewed (Oxford University Press), 2004. Regression discontinuity on close union elections: the estimate applies to establishments near the 50 percent threshold, and the authors say unions were 'somewhat unsuccessful' at winning wage gains in recent decades. Frandsen (EV-WRK-162) finds that close elections show nonrandom selection and reaches different results; Knepper (EV-WRK-163) finds effects on benefits.

statement: Frandsen (2021) found that close union elections show substantial nonrandom selection, and that after accounting for it unionization substantially decreases payroll, employment, average worker earnings and establishment survival, with worker-level earnings effects small.
anchor: Estimates accounting for this selection show that unionization substantially decreases payroll, employment, average worker earnings, and establishment survival.
Payroll and earnings decreases are driven by composition changes, with older and higher-paid workers leaving unionizing establishments and younger workers joining or staying.
Worker-level effects on earnings are small
context: Journal of Labor Economics, peer reviewed (University of Chicago Press), 2021. Regression discontinuity on matched employer-employee administrative data; the author reports manipulation of close elections, which he addresses with a panel differencing approach that others may dispute. Contests DiNardo and Lee (EV-WRK-161); the establishment-level declines are for marginal elections only and are driven by worker composition, not wage cuts for stayers. Management-aligned groups cite it against unionization.

statement: Knepper (2020) used a regression discontinuity in majority-rule union elections with firm-level data and found that after unionization average employee compensation and employer pension contributions rise, which raises the labor share of compensation, arguing that bargaining targets fringe benefits rather than wages.
anchor: Conventional wisdom suggests that labor unions raise worker wages, while the newer empirical literature finds only negligible earnings effects. I reconcile this apparent contradiction by arguing that collective bargaining targets fringe benefits.
Following unionization, average employee compensation and employer pension contributions increase, which raises the labor share of compensation.
context: Review of Economics and Statistics, peer reviewed (MIT Press), 2020. Author at the Bureau of Economic Analysis; uses BEA Multinational Enterprise Survey and Compustat, which cover larger firms, so results may not extend to small employers. Reconciles DiNardo and Lee (EV-WRK-161), which found wages near zero, with a union premium in total compensation.

statement: Farber, Herbst, Kuziemko and Naidu (2021) built survey microdata on union membership back to 1936 and found that the household union premium held between 10 and 20 log points despite large changes in density, and that unions reduce inequality, explaining a significant share of the fall in inequality between the mid-1930s and late 1940s.
anchor: We develop a new source of microdata on union membership dating back to 1936, survey data primarily from Gallup (N ≈ 980,000)
the household union premium holds relatively steady between 10 and 20 log points.
we find consistent evidence that unions reduce inequality, explaining a significant share of the dramatic fall in inequality between the mid-1930s and late 1940s.
context: Quarterly Journal of Economics, peer reviewed (Oxford University Press), 2021. Household union premium from opinion-poll microdata (mostly Gallup), not worker wages; identification uses the 1935 legalization of unions and the World War II War Labor Board, which rests on historical assumptions. The long-run relationship need not carry over to a different labor market today.

statement: Fortin, Lemieux and Lloyd found that right-to-work laws lower wages and unionization rates, using an event study of adoptions in five U.S. states since 2011 and a differential exposure design; their preferred instrumental-variable estimate of the union wage effect is 0.35 against an OLS estimate of 0.16, which they say suggests right-to-work may also affect wages directly through a weaker union threat effect.
anchor: The first approach uses an event study design to analyze the impact of the adoption of RTW laws in five U.S. states since 2011.
Both approaches indicate that RTW laws lower wages and unionization rates.

In our preferred specification based on the differential exposure design, the IV estimate of the effect of unions on wages is 0.35, which substantially exceeds the corresponding OLS estimate of 0.16. This large wage effect suggests that RTW may also directly affect wages due to a reduced union threat effect.
context: NBER working paper, 2022 (later published in Research in Labor Economics, 2023); quasi-experimental but not peer reviewed in this form. The authors note that right-to-work is not a clean instrument if it also lowers non-union wages. Contested by the Oklahoma synthetic control (EV-WRK-166), which found no wage effect, and by Heritage and Mackinac analyses of cost-of-living-adjusted wages (see notes).

statement: Eren and Ozbeklik (2016) used a synthetic control for Oklahoma and found that its right-to-work law decreased private-sector unionization rates, while the total employment rate and private-sector average wages were not affected.
anchor: the passage of RTW laws in Oklahoma decreased private sector unionization rates. Several other state outcomes including total employment rate and private sector average wages, on the other hand, were not affected by RTW laws.
context: Journal of Policy Analysis and Management, peer reviewed (Wiley), 2016. Single-state case (Oklahoma, 2001 constitutional amendment) with synthetic control weights; one treated unit limits precision, and the wage result differs from Fortin, Lemieux and Lloyd (EV-WRK-165), which uses five later adopters. Often cited by right-to-work proponents for the no-harm-to-wages finding; the unionization result is the same in both.

statement: Hirsch's review concluded that U.S. unionism has highly variable effects on productivity that are almost certainly small and insufficient to offset higher union compensation costs, that union companies have lower profitability, and that unions are associated with slower employment growth but with little difference in business failure or survival.
anchor: Rather, it appears that unionism in the US is associated with highly variable effects on productivity that on average may (or may not) be positive, but are almost certainly small and insufficient to offset higher union compensation costs.
Evidence on unions and profits is reasonably clear-cut, indicating lower profitability in union than in nonunion companies.

In short, the rather limited empirical literature that exists finds that US unions are associated with slower employment growth, but appear to exhibit little difference in rates of business failure or survival.
locator: Sections on productivity, profits and business failure
context: IZA discussion paper (2010) by Barry Hirsch, later a handbook chapter; a literature review by an economist who is a leading skeptic of union effects on firm performance. The paper says its evidence is dated and arguably unable to identify truly causal effects. It reports that DiNardo and Lee (EV-WRK-161) find negligible survival effects, while Frandsen (EV-WRK-162) later finds lower survival.

statement: Riddell (2004) used British Columbia's 1984 introduction of mandatory elections and 1993 return to card check, covering over 6,500 private-sector certifications, and found success rates fell by an average of 19 percentage points under voting and rose by about the same amount when card check returned, with management opposition about twice as effective under elections.
anchor: using data on over 6,500 private sector certifications from British Columbia over the years 1978–98.
first, in 1984, the introduction of mandatory elections; and second, in 1993, the repeal of elections and their replacement by the original card-check procedure.
Success rates declined by an average of 19 percentage points during the voting regime, and then increased by about the same amount when card-checks were re-instituted.
management opposition was twice as effective under elections as under card-checks.
context: ILR Review, peer reviewed (Cornell ILR School), 2004. Quasi-experimental before-and-after design in one province with two law changes; closest natural experiment for the card-check question, but Canadian unions, employers and enforcement differ from U.S. practice and card check there sits beside other protections. Heritage's reading of NLRB data (EV-WRK-123) puts employer coercion at lower rates than EPI's (EV-WRK-121).

statement: Johnson (2010) used a panel of Canadian jurisdictions that adopted first contract arbitration at different times and found that the legislation reduces first-agreement work stoppage incidence by at least 50 percent, is used infrequently with first contracts rarely imposed, and has no statistically significant effect on the duration of first-agreement stoppages.
anchor: First, the author finds that the presence of FCA legislation reduces first agreement work stoppage incidence by at least 50 percent. Descriptive measures reveal that FCA is accessed infrequently; it is even rarer for a first contract (in whole or in part) to be imposed.
Finally, first contract arbitration has no statistically significant impact on the duration of first agreement work stoppages.
context: ILR Review, peer reviewed (Cornell ILR School), 2010; the quotation is the corrected abstract. Provincial panel, so effects are on stoppages, not on the share of units reaching a first contract or on later contract quality; the finding that FCA 'encourages collective bargaining' is the author's inference from low use. Written when the Employee Free Choice Act was pending. Canadian arbitration design (who may request, standards for imposing terms) differs from the PRO Act's.

statement: Cramton, Gunderson and Tracy used large Canadian private-sector contract negotiations from January 1967 to March 1993 and found that prohibiting replacement workers during strikes is associated with significantly higher wages and more frequent and longer strikes, and that union workers are better off with a ban because the higher wage more than compensates for the longer strikes.
anchor: Using Canadian data on large, private-sector contract negotiations from January 1967 to March 1993, we find that wages and strikes are substantially influenced by labor policy. In particular, we find that prohibiting the use of replacement workers during strikes is associated with significantly higher wages, and more frequent and longer strikes.
Despite the higher dispute costs, union workers are better off with a ban on replacement workers. The higher wage more than compensates for the more frequent and longer strikes.
context: NBER working paper, 1995, published in the Review of Economics and Statistics (1999). Provincial variation in anti-replacement laws, contracts of 500 or more workers only. Budd (EV-WRK-171) finds little effect of banning permanent replacements on incidence, duration or wages; Quebec's 1977 law dominates the identification, so results may reflect other Quebec changes.

statement: Budd (1996) used Canadian manufacturing collective-bargaining agreements and found that a general ban on strike replacements is associated with longer strikes, but found little evidence that banning permanent strike replacements significantly influences strike incidence, strike duration or negotiated wages.
anchor: Although a general ban on strike replacements is found to be associated with longer strikes, little evidence is found to suggest that banning permanent strike replacements significantly influences strike incidence, strike duration, or negotiated wages.
context: Industrial Relations, peer reviewed (Wiley), 1996. Manufacturing agreements only. Distinguishes bans on permanent replacements (the U.S. question under the PRO Act) from general bans on any replacement; Cramton, Gunderson and Tracy (EV-WRK-170) pool provincial bans and find higher wages and longer strikes.

statement: Canada's Bill C-58 received royal assent on June 20, 2024 and its amendments to the Canada Labour Code took effect on June 20, 2025; employers in federally regulated workplaces are banned from using contractors or specified other people to do the work of striking or locked-out workers, and a violation can be prosecuted with a fine of up to $100,000 per day.
anchor: On June 20, 2025, amendments to Part I of the Code and the Canada Industrial Relations Board Regulations, 2012, that were proposed through Bill C-58, An Act to amend the Canada Labour Code and the Canada Industrial Relations Board Regulations, 2012, which received royal assent on June 20, 2024, came into effect.
Employers are also prohibited from using contractors to fill in and do union work during a strike or lockout, regardless of when they were hired.
Violating the prohibitions can be made an offence, and, if prosecuted and convicted, an employer can be subject to a fine of up to $100,000 per day.
locator: Description of first component and enforcement
context: Government of Canada backgrounder (Employment and Social Development Canada), June 2025; a summary of the statute, not its text; the government supported the bill. Applies to federally regulated sectors only (air, rail, road and marine transport, banks, telecommunications and postal services), not provincial workplaces; British Columbia and Quebec had older provincial bans. The ban is under 18 months old, so no evaluation of its effects was found.

statement: The OECD (2019), using country-level data for 35 OECD countries between 1980 and 2016, found coordinated bargaining systems, including organised decentralisation, linked with higher employment and lower unemployment than fully decentralised systems, wage dispersion smallest among workers covered by sectoral bargaining, and lower productivity growth in centralised systems when coverage is high.
anchor: co-ordinated systems – including those characterised by organised decentralisation – are linked with higher employment and lower unemployment (also for young people, women and low-skilled workers) than fully decentralised systems.
wage dispersion is on average smallest among workers who are covered by sectoral bargaining.
Centralised bargaining systems tend to be associated with lower productivity growth if coverage of agreements is high.
using country-level data on labour market outcomes for 35 OECD countries between 1980 and 2016
locator: Chapter 'The role of collective bargaining systems for labour market performance', main empirical findings and conclusion
context: OECD, 2019. Cross-country regressions on 35 countries; associations, not causal estimates, and the sample cannot say what happens when a country with firm-level bargaining like the United States adds sectoral bargaining. Countries with sectoral systems differ in many other institutions. The OECD site blocked download, so the licence was not checked.

statement: The OECD (2019) said that where sectoral bargaining lacks broad-based representation, administrative extension of agreements can help cover firms and workers who do not take part, and that extension should be limited by representativeness criteria, a public-interest test, and exemptions or opt-outs for firms in serious economic hardship.
anchor: In systems with sectoral bargaining and no broad-based representation, administrative extensions can help cover companies and workers not participating in collective bargaining.

This can be achieved by subjecting extension requests to reasonable representativeness criteria and a meaningful test of public interest and providing well-defined procedures for exemptions and opt-outs of firms in case of serious economic hardship.
locator: Chapter conclusions on coverage and extension
context: OECD secretariat recommendation, 2019, drawn from the experience of continental European countries with extension rules; a design guideline from an international organization, not an evaluation. New Zealand's Fair Pay Agreements (EV-WRK-175) show a case in which a negotiated extension model was repealed before any agreement was finalised.

statement: The Institute for Government reports that New Zealand's Fair Pay Agreements Act came into force on 1 December 2022 and was swiftly repealed a year later by the new coalition after the 2023 election; six sectors had approval to initiate bargaining but none got far, no pay settlements were finalised, and FPAs faced stiff opposition from employers over cost and flexibility.
anchor: came into force on 1 December 2022. However, the act was swiftly repealed a year later by the new right-wing coalition that came to power after the 2023 general election.

At the time six sectors, including bus drivers, commercial cleaners and early childhood education workers, had received approval to initiate bargaining under the new system. However, none had got far, and no pay settlements were finalised before the legislation was repealed.
FPAs faced stiff opposition from the off, particularly from employers due to concerns about cost and flexibility.
context: Institute for Government, a UK nonpartisan think tank, July 2024, writing about lessons for a UK Labour plan; a secondary account of New Zealand events. The Act's repeal took effect 20 December 2023 (Employment New Zealand; New Zealand Legislation). Employers, led by BusinessNZ, opposed the system; the unions' side says the repeal ended agreements already near conclusion. A failure-of-durability case: the system lasted about a year and produced no agreement.

statement: CBO estimated that the Protecting the Right to Organize Act as ordered reported in 2019 would let the NLRB assess civil penalties of up to $50,000 for an unfair labor practice and up to $100,000 for discriminatory discharge, imposed in about 120 cases a year, one-quarter at the higher rate, raising revenues by $39 million over 2020-2029.
anchor: enable the NLRB to assess a civil penalty of up to $50,000 on employers that commit an unfair labor practice as defined by the NLRA and up to $100,000 on employers that specifically discriminate against or discharge an employee because of membership in a labor organization.
CBO estimates those penalties would be imposed in about 120 cases per year, about one-quarter of which would be subject to the higher penalty.
CBO estimates that enacting those provisions would increase revenues by $39 million over the 2020-2029 period.
context: Congressional Budget Office (nonpartisan), December 2019, for the House committee-reported H.R. 2474; no CBO estimate was found for H.R. 842 (2021) or H.R. 20 (2025). The estimate scores budget effects from existing case counts and does not model how penalties change employer behavior; CBO lists predicting employer responses as a significant uncertainty. Penalty amounts match the introduced text in EV-WRK-142.

statement: CBO reported that the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service receives around 500 NLRB notifications a year of newly certified units working toward a first agreement, and mediates only when both parties request it, which occurs in roughly 10 percent of initial collective bargaining cases.
anchor: Currently, FMCS receives around 500 notifications annually from the NLRB that new bargaining units have been certified and that the parties are working toward an initial collective bargaining agreement. The agency mediates disputes only if both parties request its services, which occurs in roughly 10 percent of initial collective bargaining cases.
locator: Basis of Estimate, Spending Subject to Appropriation, FMCS
context: CBO (nonpartisan) reporting FMCS figures supplied by the agency, December 2019; the counts predate the 2024-2026 rise in NLRB petitions (EV-WRK-109).

statement: EPI's July 2026 inventory reports that Nevada's home care board made recommendations in 2022 that helped pave the way for 2023 legislation setting a $16 minimum wage for home care workers, and that Colorado's Direct Care Workforce Stabilization Board recommended $25 an hour by 2026 in 2024 while 2025 legislation set a $17 minimum wage.
anchor: Board recommendations in 2022 helped pave way for 2023 legislation setting $16 min wage for home care workers and increasing Medicaid reimbursement rates.
2024 board recommendations laid groundwork for 2025 legislation including min wage of $17 for direct care workers (board recommendation was $25/hr by 2026)
locator: Appendix table, Nevada and Colorado rows, 'Notable outcomes'
context: EPI, July 2026; a labor-aligned think tank that favors sectoral bargaining and wage boards. The table's 'notable outcomes' text is EPI's characterization; the boards were advisory and the legislature set the wages, at $17 against a board recommendation of $25 in Colorado, which shows an advisory board's recommendation can be cut. Primary board reports (Nevada Home Care Employment Standards Board 2022 report) were not catalogued.

statement: EPI's table describes Minnesota's Nursing Home Workforce Standards Board as nine members, the commissioners of labor, health and human services plus six governor appointees split evenly between worker and employer representatives, whose first rules in 2024 included 1.5x pay for designated holidays and one hour of required 'know your rights' training every two years.
anchor: Nine-member board, including commissioners of state Dept of Labor, Dept of Health, and Dept of Human Services, plus six members appointed by governor: three representing nursing home workers or worker organizations and three representing nursing home employers or employer organizations

First set of rules issued by board in 2024 included 1.5x pay for designated holidays, min wage of $19 in 2026 and $20.50 in 2027 (pending federal approval), and one hour of required “know your rights” training every two years.
context: EPI, July 2026, labor-aligned; its description of the statute and rules. Wages are in EV-CAR-618. Minnesota DLI's pages (read but not catalogued) record that the board voted on the initial wage standards on May 9, 2024, published the adopted rules in the State Register on October 28, 2024 under the expedited rulemaking process, and that the wage standards took effect on September 10, 2026 only after federal approval (CMS, August 11, 2026) of a Medicaid rate increase: the board's wage power depends on public reimbursement.

statement: EPI's table describes Seattle's Domestic Workers Standards Board as a 13-member board of domestic workers, hiring entities and a community representative whose power is to consider, analyze and make recommendations to the City on protections, benefits and working conditions.
anchor: 13-member board, including four domestic workers or worker organization representatives, two domestic workers who are not worker organization representatives, four hiring entities or their representatives, two individuals who contract with or hire domestic workers, and one community representative
Consider, analyze, and make recommendations to City on legal protections, benefits, and working conditions for domestic worker industry standards
context: EPI, July 2026, labor-aligned. The board is advisory, with no power to set wages; the table lists no notable outcomes for it. City documents (read but not catalogued) say the board was created in 2019 and that the City Council committee must respond to its recommendations within 120 days.

statement: EPI's table reports that Detroit's Industry Standards Board ordinance creates a nine-person board once at least 150 workers in an industry petition, with authority to conduct outreach, investigate local conditions and report recommendations to City Council, and that the first board, for sports arena workers, issued recommendations in November 2025.
anchor: Once triggered (by petition from at least 150 workers in a given industry), ordinance requires creation of nine-person board
Boards established for a particular industry have authority to conduct outreach, investigate local working conditions, and report recommendations to City Council.
The first board created under the ordinance for Sports Arena Workers issued its recommendations to the council in November, 2025.
context: EPI, July 2026, labor-aligned. A worker-petition trigger and advisory powers; the table does not say whether the Council acted on the recommendations.

statement: EPI's table reports that New York's Farm Laborers Wage Board, a three-person board with one farm bureau, one state AFL-CIO and one commissioner-appointed member, issued 2022 recommendations that the state adopted in 2023, starting a 10-year phase-in that lowers the farmworker overtime threshold from 60 to 40 hours a week by January 1, 2032.
anchor: Three-person board, including one representative of farm bureau, one representative of state AFL-CIO, and one representative appointed by state Labor Commissioner
Board’s 2022 recommendations were adopted by state in 2023, starting 10-year phase in to lower the current 60-hour threshold for farmworker overtime pay to 40 hours per week by January 1, 2032
locator: Appendix table, New York Farm Laborers Wage Board row
context: EPI, July 2026, labor-aligned. An example of a tripartite board whose recommendation was adopted in full by the state but on a slow phase-in.

statement: Australia's Fair Work Commission said in 2025 that approximately 20.7 per cent of all employees are paid the minimum rates in its 121 modern awards, that their wages are only about 10.5 per cent of the national wage bill, and it raised the National Minimum Wage and all modern award minimum rates 3.5 per cent from 1 July 2025.
anchor: Approximately 20.7 per cent of all employees in Australia are paid at the applicable minimum wage rates in the 121 modern industry and occupational awards currently in operation.
the wages paid to them constitute only about 10.5 per cent of the national ‘wage bill’.
The decision we have made is to increase the National Minimum Wage and all modern award minimum wage rates by 3.5 per cent, effective from 1 July 2025.
context: Fair Work Commission Expert Panel, an independent tribunal, June 2025 (Albanese government period). The awards set minimum rates by industry or occupation through a quasi-judicial annual review, a sectoral minimum-standards system separate from enterprise agreements. The 2026 review (2 June 2026) raised award wages 4.75 per cent per the Fair Work Ombudsman; the next review is expected in June 2027.

statement: Jäger, Noy and Schoefer (2022) reviewed codetermination, meaning worker representation in firms' governance, and concluded that micro evidence points to zero or small positive effects on worker and firm outcomes, and that new country-level event studies of reforms between the 1960s and 2010s find no effects on aggregate economic outcomes or the quality of industrial relations.
anchor: The available micro evidence points to zero or small positive effects of codetermination on worker and firm outcomes and leaves room for moderate positive effects on productivity, wages, and job stability.

The authors also present new country-level, general-equilibrium event studies of codetermination reforms between the 1960s and 2010s, finding no effects on aggregate economic outcomes or the quality of industrial relations.
context: ILR Review, peer reviewed (Cornell ILR School), 2022. A review plus new cross-country event studies; board-level codetermination, not bargaining. The authors attribute the limited impact partly to weak worker authority and to interaction with unions and collective bargaining. The companion Germany study (Jager, Schoefer and Heining, QJE 2021) finds no wage effects of the one-third board mandate (read in an Exa extract, not catalogued).

statement: A law-firm blog reported in September 2025 that 12 states had enacted laws to ban or restrict captive audience meetings, that Minnesota's 2023 law gives aggrieved employees a private right of action, and that on September 3 the 8th Circuit reversed the district court and dismissed the challenge to it, leaving the NLRA preemption and First Amendment questions unresolved.
anchor: There are now 12 states, including Minnesota, which have enacted laws designed to ban or restrict captive audience meetings: Alaska, Connecticut, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, Vermont, Washington, and, most recently, California.
The Minnesota legislature adopted a law in 2023
It provides a private right of action for “aggrieved employee[s],”
In a decision issued on September 3, the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals reversed the district court.
The issue of whether the law is preempted by the NLRA or the First Amendment remains unresolved.
locator: Paragraphs on the 12 states, the Minnesota Act and the 8th Circuit decision
context: Employment-law firm blog, September 2025; a secondary legal summary with a management-side perspective. The dismissal turned on sovereign immunity and the state officials' disavowal of enforcement, not on the merits. A Bloomberg Law item of September 2025 counted at least five challenges in four states (California, Connecticut, Illinois, Minnesota); California's SB 399 was preliminarily enjoined on First Amendment and preemption grounds in September 2025 (not catalogued here for lack of a source ID). The NLRB's own Amazon.com Services ruling is in EV-WRK-127.

statement: A New York appeals court described the 2015 Fast Food Wage Board as three members, one each for employers, employees and the general public, whose July 2015 report recommended a gradual phase-in reaching full effect on December 31, 2018 in New York City and July 1, 2021 elsewhere, limited to chains with at least 30 establishments nationally, which the Commissioner accepted in full in September 2015.
anchor: The Commissioner proceeded to name a three-member wage board with one representative each for the interests of employers, employees and the general public
The wage board suggested a gradual phase-in of the increase, which would take full effect on December 31, 2018 in New York City and July 1, 2021 elsewhere in the state.
The recommended increase was additionally limited to fast-food workers employed by fast-food establishments in New York that were part of a chain with at least 30
In September 2015, the Commissioner accepted the report in full and ordered that the recommended minimum wage increase be implemented
locator: Opinion, background and first Discussion paragraph
context: Appellate Division, Third Department, June 2016, a court's account of the administrative record; it confirmed the wage order on appeal. The target wage ($15) and the wage-board model were later overtaken by the 2016 statutory $15 minimum, which the court says removed the Commissioner's power to set higher occupational minimums above the new statutory rates. That curtailment of future boards is a durability point; no evaluation of the wage order's employment effects was found.

statement: In a natural field experiment, Levine, Toffel and Johnson compared 409 randomly inspected California establishments with 409 matched controls and found a 9.4% decline in injury rates and a 26% reduction in injury cost, with no evidence of losses in employment, sales, credit ratings or firm survival.
anchor: We compared 409 randomly inspected establishments in California with 409 matched-control establishments that were eligible, but not chosen, for inspection.
randomly inspected employers experienced a 9.4% decline in injury rates
a 26% reduction in injury cost
We find no evidence that these improvements came at the expense of employment, sales, credit ratings, or firm survival.
context: Science (AAAS), peer reviewed, May 2012; academic authors (Berkeley, Harvard Business School, Duke), no stakeholder funding noted in the extract. Quasi-experimental: Cal/OSHA's random allocation of some inspections gives a matched-control comparison. Limits stated in the paper's text: a subset of firms in one state, and it ignores any effect of the threat of inspection on uninspected workplaces. Read through an HBS-hosted copy of the article as well as the abstract. No independent publisher's replication is in the register; the same authors' later AEJ: Applied paper (Johnson, Levine and Toffel 2023, not drafted here for lack of a source ID) reports 2.4 fewer serious injuries (9 percent) per inspection over five years.

statement: Levine, Toffel and Johnson's point estimates imply the injury reductions in the 5 years after a Cal/OSHA inspection cut medical costs and lost earnings by roughly $355,000 (in 2011 dollars), and they can be 95% certain the mean inspected establishment either grows payroll or loses less than $221,000 over the 5 years.
anchor: reduced medical costs and lost earnings by roughly $355,000 (in 2011 dollars)
we can be 95% certain that the mean establishment either grows payroll or experiences a decline of less than $221,000 over the 5 years
there is substantial uncertainty about our estimated benefits
context: Same Science article as EV-WRK-249, same authors, so not independent of it. The paper calls these numbers 'with many assumptions' and notes substantial uncertainty in the benefit estimate; the payroll bound and the benefit are in different units. Single-establishment firms in California only. Quotations read through the HBS-hosted PDF; its text has line-break artifacts, so check against the journal page.

statement: Johnson found that OSHA press releases about violators, begun in 2009, led to 73 percent fewer violations at peer facilities in the same sector within a 5 kilometer radius, and that OSHA would need 210 additional inspections to match the compliance gain from a single press release.
anchor: In 2009, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) began issuing press releases about facilities that violated safety and health regulations.
A press release leads to 73 percent fewer violations at “peer” facilities in the same sector within a 5 kilometer radius.
OSHA would need to conduct 210 additional inspections to achieve the same improvement in compliance as achieved with a single press release.
context: American Economic Review, peer reviewed (June 2020); regression discontinuity around a cutoff rule OSHA used for issuing releases (Obama administration policy, 2009 onward). The paper says the injury result is 'substantial, but the estimate is somewhat imprecise', and that compliance gains appeared where unions were strong and not where they were weak, which it reads as employers avoiding costly responses from workers. The 210-inspection comparison depends on the paper's cost assumptions. Same lead author as EV-WRK-249; not independent of it.

statement: Galvin's study of state wage-theft laws, summarized in a 2017 policy brief, found that the introduction of treble damages had the greatest deterrent effect, with statistically significant drops in violation rates in five states, and that effective policy needed favorable partisan majorities, determined coalitions of workers' advocates and strong enforcement of penalties.
anchor: the introduction of treble damages has the greatest deterrent effect
The implementation of “treble damages” in five states led to statistically significant drops in violation rates.

However, effective policies require three conditions: favorable partisan majorities in state government, determined coalitions of workers’ advocates lobbying for change, and strong enforcement of penalties.
context: Northwestern University's Institute for Policy Research (academic), July 2017, summarizing Galvin's peer-reviewed article in Perspectives on Politics 14(2), 2016 (the brief, not the article, was read; the article's abstract reports difference-in-differences analyses of a dozen state laws and that 'the structure of the policy matters a great deal, as does its enforcement'). Violation rates are estimated from Current Population Survey wage data, so they carry measurement error; the five-state treble-damages result is a small-sample difference-in-differences. The brief's own wording is 'five states' while the abstract says a dozen laws were examined. The project brief called this an ILR Review paper; it is Perspectives on Politics.

statement: Weil and Pyles, analyzing complaint activity under the FLSA and OSHA, found a significant gap between the level of complaint activity and underlying violation rates, and concluded that silence should not be confused with compliance and that enforcement must focus where workers are unlikely to complain.
anchor: We show that there is a significant gap between the level of complaint activity and underlying violation rates.
silence should not be confused with compliance
Workplace regulatory policy must focus on workplaces where big problems exist but also where workers are unlikely to complain because of barriers they face.
context: Comparative Labor Law & Policy Journal 27, 2005; peer reviewed (law and policy journal). Uses survey data on violations and agency data on complaints from before 2005, by industry, so it shows an industry-level mismatch rather than a measured effect of any policy. David Weil later led the Wage and Hour Division (2014-2017, Obama administration) and built its strategic-enforcement approach on this research, so the authors are not neutral about the remedy. Read through the authors' posted PDF.

statement: In a 2008 survey of 4,387 workers in low-wage industries in Chicago, Los Angeles and New York City, 43 percent of those who had complained or tried to form a union experienced retaliation that the report calls illegal, and another 20 percent who had a serious problem did not complain, half of them for fear of losing their job.
anchor: In 2008, we conducted a landmark survey of 4,387 workers in low-wage industries in the three largest U.S. cities
Of those, 43 percent experienced one or more forms of illegal retaliation from their employer or supervisor.

Another 20 percent of workers reported that they did not make a complaint to their employer during the past 12 months, even though they had experienced a serious problem such as dangerous working conditions or not being paid the minimum wage.
Half were afraid of losing their job, 10 percent were afraid they would have their hours or wages cut, and 36 percent thought it would not make a difference.
context: National Employment Law Project, a worker-advocacy organization, with university researchers; September 2009; not peer reviewed. Respondent-driven sampling of front-line low-wage workers in three cities in 2008, weighted to about 1.64 million workers; the sample is not national. A reanalysis of the raw survey (Alexander and Prasad, Indiana Law Journal 2014) describes the 43 percent as employer reprisal of any kind after a complaint, of which it reads roughly 35 percent as unlawful retaliation, so the 'illegal' label should be checked before the figure is repeated (read only through a search extract of that article).

statement: OSHA's August 2024 proposed heat standard estimated annualized costs of 7.8 billion (2 percent discount rate, ten-year period) against total annual benefits of $9.179 billion, preventing 531 of an estimated 559 annual heat fatalities and 16,027 of 24,656 annual heat-related injuries and illnesses.

OSHA
estimates that annualized costs, using a 2 percent discount rate over a
ten-year period, would equal 7.8 billion.

Total benefits each year
for avoided heat-related fatalities and HRIs are $9.179 billion.

The parameters used to
estimate the magnitude of underreporting of HRIs and the effectiveness
of the proposed standard have considerable uncertainty.
locator: Preamble, Section VIII (Preliminary Economic Analysis): summary, total costs and benefits
context: Labor Department (OSHA), Biden administration, proposed rule of August 30, 2024 (89 FR 70698), Preliminary Economic Analysis; a proposal, not a final rule, and the Trump administration's current agenda lists a supplemental notice (see EV-WRK-237). The benefit total rests on OSHA's own undercount adjustment (559 deaths against far fewer reported) and on an assumed effectiveness of the standard, which the proposal itself says carry considerable uncertainty; the dollar split of the $9.179 billion between deaths and injuries was not checked here. Industry commenters contest the analysis (U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the National Association of Home Builders ask for withdrawal; an American Enterprise Institute paper argues the benefit is overstated); those comments were read through search extracts and are listed in the notes, not drafted for lack of source IDs.

context: OSHA's description of state law in its own proposal (Labor Department, Biden administration, 2024); the dates are the citation years of the state rules as OSHA lists them, not necessarily effective dates.

statement: Park, Pankratz and Behrer, using the universe of California workers' compensation injury claims for 2001-2018, found that hotter temperature causes approximately 20,000 injuries per year, in indoor as well as outdoor settings and for injury types unrelated to temperature, and that the heat-sensitivity of injuries declined over the period.
anchor: Using data covering the universe of injury claims from the nation's largest worker's compensation system (2001-2018)
Hotter temperature increases workplace injuries significantly, causing approximately 20,000 injuries per year.
The effects persist in both outdoor and indoor settings (e.g. manufacturing, warehousing), and for injury types ostensibly unrelated to temperature (e.g. falling from heights)
We document a decline in the heat-sensitivity of injuries over the study period, suggesting significant scope for adaptation using existing technologies.
context: IZA Institute of Labor Economics discussion paper by UCLA and Stanford authors (posted July 2021, last revised May 2025 per the SSRN listing); not shown as peer reviewed in the extract. Identifies effects from day-to-day weather variation within ZIP codes against claims filed, so it counts compensated injuries only; the paper does not separate effects of the 2005 heat standard from other adaptation. Other write-ups of the same paper report a range of 15,000 to 25,000 injuries a year and a 6 to 9 percent higher injury risk above 90 degrees (UCLA and Equitable Growth summaries, not drafted).

statement: Fomenko, McInerney and Negrusa, using a triple-differences design on workers' compensation data, estimated that California's heat standard, adopted in 2005, reduced injuries on hot days by 15-17 percent in construction, 19-25 percent in transportation and 24-27 percent in agriculture, with the transportation and rate-based estimates more sensitive to specification.
anchor: we evaluate California’s heat standard – adopted in 2005 - and find that the standard substantially reduces the frequency of work injuries in the construction, agriculture, and transportation industries
ranging from 15–17 percent in construction, to 19-25 percent in transportation, and to 24–27 percent in agriculture
Dean and McCallum (2025) provide suggestive evidence that heat-related deaths fell for outdoor workers in California after the heat standard was introduced.

Specifications that estimate the rate of injuries or rely on an alternative approach are more sensitive, which may reflect changes in the transportation industry or increased noise due to the lower incidence of injury.
context: NBER Working Paper 35772 (September 2026; 'Cooler Laws, Safer Workers'), not peer reviewed. Hot-versus-cool days, high-risk versus low-risk industries, before versus after the standard; counts of injuries, with the paper reporting rate-based specifications as less stable. California only; the standard was revised in 2010 and 2015 and was made permanent in 2006, so the estimate pools versions. A Health Affairs 2025 study of heat deaths (Dean and McCallum) found no decline in 2005-09 and point estimates of 33 and 51 percent reductions after 2010 and 2015 that were not individually significant (read through an extract; not drafted for lack of a source ID).

statement: Palagashvili, Suarez, Kaiser and Melo estimated that, after California's AB5 and relative to other states, self-employment fell by 10.5 percent and overall employment by 4.4 percent on average in nonexempt occupations, and found no robust evidence that traditional employment rose.
anchor: Our estimates indicate that self-employment fell by 10.5 percent on average for nonexempt occupations, while overall employment fell by 4.4 percent on average for nonexempt occupations.
We find no robust evidence that traditional employment increased post-AB5.
We employ a simple difference-in-difference strategy to compare labor market outcomes in occupations within California to those outside California before and after AB5 was enacted.
context: Mercatus Center at George Mason University working paper (January 2024), a market-oriented research center; not peer reviewed in this form. Current Population Survey data by state, occupation and month with other states as controls. Critics quoted by Bloomberg Law (Michael Reich of UC Berkeley, Heidi Shierholz of EPI) say it ignores differing pre-trends and that a fall in traditional employment is hard to explain; the lead author has said the paper cannot be interpreted causally given noisy data and reports associations (Labor Market Matters post, January 2024; read through search extracts). It covers only nonexempt occupations, not all of California. Abstract read through the SSRN listing, results text through a copy of the working paper.

statement: In the quartile of occupations with the highest prevalence of self-employment, the same Mercatus study found that reclassification increased traditional employment by 10.2 percent and decreased self-employment by 17.7 percent, with no significant effect on overall employment, and that AB5 may have increased traditional employment only there.
anchor: Lastly, among occupations in the highest quartile of prevalence of self-employment, we find a statistically insignificant association between worker reclassification and overall employment and labor force participation.
We find that worker reclassification increased traditional employment by 10.2 percent, while it decreased self-employment by 17.7 percent
AB5 may have increased traditional employment only among occupations in the highest quartile of prevalence of self-employment while decreasing traditional employment in the remaining quartiles.
context: Same Mercatus working paper as EV-WRK-259 (same authors, so not independent of it); the finding is the paper's own qualification of its headline, in the occupations where misclassification is most likely. Subgroup estimates from one difference-in-differences design; noisy and subject to the pre-trend concerns noted at EV-WRK-259. Read through a copy of the working paper.

statement: The Economic Policy Institute reports that a 2004 Harvard Labor and Worklife Program study found 14% to 24% of Massachusetts construction employers misclassified workers as independent contractors, costing the state up to $152 million in lost income taxes, up to $35 million in lost unemployment insurance premiums and up to $91 million in unpaid workers' compensation premiums, and that experts in the state think the ABC test signed into law later that year improved compliance and reduced misclassification.
anchor: A major study from the Harvard Labor and Worklife Program in 2004 showed widespread misclassification

14% to 24% of all construction employers in Massachusetts misclassified construction workers as independent contractors, costing the state up to $152 million in lost income taxes, up to $35 million in lost unemployment insurance premiums, and up to $91 million in unpaid workers’ compensation premiums
Republican Gov. Mitt Romney signed the bill into law later that year.
Experts in the state think adoption of the ABC test has improved legal compliance and reduced misclassification.
context: EPI, a labor-aligned think tank, June 2021, a policy paper defending the ABC test; the dollar figures are the upper ends of ranges from the 2004 Harvard study (extrapolated from state audits, with an assumed 30 to 50 percent of misclassified workers' income unreported), and the claim that the ABC test reduced misclassification is expert opinion, not a measured effect. It was published before the 2024 Mercatus estimates that ABC tests lowered employment (EV-WRK-259) and does not answer them. Read through a search extract.

statement: California's Proposition 22, enacted by voters on November 3, 2020, makes app-based drivers for companies such as Uber, Lyft and DoorDash independent contractors, not employees, when several conditions are met, and on July 25, 2024 the California Supreme Court affirmed that this classification (section 7451) does not conflict with article XIV, section 4 of the state constitution on workers' compensation.
