statement: Arnold, Quach and Taska found, using a difference-in-differences design on state laws requiring salary information in job postings, that employers increased the fraction of postings with salary information by 30 percentage points and that wages rose 1.3-3.6%, with no impacts on pay dispersion, employment, the number of postings, or skill and education requirements.
anchor: employers increased the fraction of postings with salary information by 30 percentage points
we find consistent evidence of an increase in wages of 1.3-3.6%
We find no impacts on pay dispersion, employment, the number of postings, or skill and education requirements.
context: NBER working paper (November 2025 version), not shown as peer reviewed; academic authors with job-posting data from a commercial vendor. The earlier versions and the January 2025 manuscript focus on Colorado's January 2021 posting law (about 30 points more postings with pay information, substantial non-compliance, fines of $500 to $10,000 rarely imposed) and report wage gains of about 1.3 to 3.6 percent from postings, Glassdoor and payroll data; the 2022 version reported a 3.6 percent rise in posted salaries for employers that posted before and after. The wage effects are identified from comparison states and the authors read them as more competition for workers; the mechanism is not directly tested. Opposing evidence: EV-WRK-408 (a different law).

statement: Cullen and Pakzad-Hurson model that transparency reduces workers' individual bargaining power and leads to lower average wages, and find that U.S. state laws protecting workers' right to share salary information lead wages to decline by approximately 2%, with the smallest declines where workers have low individual bargaining power.
anchor: Our model predicts that transparency reduces the individual bargaining power of workers, leading to lower average wages.
We test our model with an event‐study analysis of U.S. state‐level laws protecting the right of private sector workers to communicate salary information with their coworkers.
transparency laws empirically lead wages to decline by approximately 2%, and wage declines are smallest in magnitude when workers have low individual bargaining power
context: Econometrica 91(3), May 2023, peer reviewed; economic theory plus an event study of state laws that protect employees who discuss pay with coworkers, not laws that require employers to post pay ranges, so it does not test the posting mandates that EV-WRK-407 studies; the authors' model implies transparency has a muted effect where individual bargaining power is low. Read through the Econometric Society abstract and the NBER working-paper version.

statement: Using stacked difference-in-differences models and original survey data, Schneider, Harknett and Arbelaez found that Fair Workweek laws increased advance notice of schedules by 13 percentage points and cut clopening shifts by 8 percentage points, with no evidence of hour increases for covered workers and no evidence of compensatory retrenchment in other aspects of job quality.
anchor: FWW regulations increased advance notice by 13 percentage points (p.p.) across all models.
workers covered by these laws experienced an 8-p.p. reduction in clopening shifts (models 2 and 3) compared with their counterparts not covered by these new laws
we find no evidence of hour increases for covered workers
We find no evidence of compensatory retrenchment in other aspects of job quality.
context: Science Advances, peer reviewed (published June 26, 2026). Pools Fair Workweek laws in several large cities and one state against comparison areas using the authors' own worker survey; two of the authors also wrote the Seattle evaluation (EV-WRK-402), so the two are not independent. Survey self-reports; the effect on last-minute timing changes (about 6 points) was less robust; shift cancellations and on-call shifts did not change; hours fell about 0.37 a week but not significantly. Quotations read through a copy of the article with line-break artifacts.

statement: In their review of earlier evaluations, Schneider, Harknett and Arbelaez report a 98-interview study concluding that Oregon's statewide scheduling law was broadly ineffective, and that studies of Oregon, New York City and two other jurisdictions found no major unintended effects on employment or hours; they write that average effects disguise substantial heterogeneity across jurisdictions.
anchor: Petrucci et al. (34) draw on 98 in-depth interviews with workers in Oregon to conclude that the law was broadly ineffective.
that laws in those two jurisdictions and Oregon and New York City did not have major unintended effects on employment and/or number of work hours.
These average effects disguise substantial heterogeneity across jurisdictions

Fair Workweek legislation has realized some intended effects on work schedules without unintended consequences, but the potential for more widespread, effective enforcement has not been fully realized.
context: Secondary summary inside the Science Advances article of EV-WRK-409: the Oregon interview study (Petrucci and co-authors, ILR Review 2021) is a qualitative study of 98 workers and managers after the 2018 law, not an effect estimate, and the null employment findings it cites for Oregon and New York City come from other authors' studies (not read directly). Oregon's law covers retail, hospitality and food service employers with 500 or more employees worldwide and lets workers go on a voluntary standby list that exempts employers from predictability pay (Urban Institute report, read through an extract; not drafted).

statement: Lipsitz and Starr, exploiting Oregon's 2008 ban on noncompete agreements for hourly-paid workers, found that the ban raised hourly wages by 2%-3% on average, that the effect on workers actually bound by noncompetes may be as great as 14%-21% though likely lower, and that it raised job-to-job mobility without affecting hours worked.
anchor: We exploit the 2008 Oregon ban on noncompete agreements (NCAs) for hourly-paid workers to provide the first evidence on the impact of NCAs on low-wage workers.
We find that banning NCAs for hourly workers increased hourly wages by 2%–3% on average.
the effect on employees actually bound by NCAs may be as great as 14%–21%, though the true effect is likely lower due to labor market spillovers onto those not bound by NCAs
The Oregon low-wage NCA ban also improved average occupational status in Oregon, raised job-to-job mobility, and increased the proportion of salaried workers without affecting hours worked.
context: Management Science 68(1), January 2022, peer reviewed (online April 2021); one-state quasi-experiment comparing Oregon hourly workers with other states; the 14%-21% figure is a scaling of the average effect by the share of hourly workers bound by noncompetes, which the authors themselves say overstates the effect. One author, Michael Lipsitz, is listed at the Federal Trade Commission, the agency that issued the 2024 noncompete rule (EV-WRK-244). Contested: EV-WRK-412.

statement: Oh Lam, Lenard and Wallsten argued that the literature the FTC cited shows mixed results on earnings, job creation, firm formation, entrepreneurship, training, investment and firm value, and does not support a ban across all sectors, occupations and industries, while allowing that investigations of noncompete use among low-wage workers may be justified.
anchor: the empirical literature on non-compete agreements cited by the FTC in its Notice for Proposed Rulemaking (“NPRM”) shows mixed results on earnings, job creation, firm formation, entrepreneurship, training, investment, and firm value
The empirical literature, in its current development, does not support a ban on non-competes in all U.S. labor sectors all-across occupations and industries.
Investigations into the use of non-competes in certain areas, like among low-wage workers, may be justified, but the research does not support such an extensive prohibition.
context: Fordham Journal of Corporate & Financial Law (a law-review comment on the FTC's January 2023 proposed rule; the publication date and the authors' institution, understood to be the Technology Policy Institute, a think tank, were not shown in the extract and should be confirmed). A critique of the FTC's cost-benefit analysis, not new estimates; its low-wage concession is consistent with the Oregon evidence in EV-WRK-411.

statement: Schmieder and von Wachter's review of 18 quasi-experimental studies of how UI benefit levels affect unemployment duration found a median duration elasticity of 0.53 (0.38 for U.S. studies alone, range 0.1 to 1.2), and cautioned that such estimates are imperfect proxies for the full disincentive effect of UI.
anchor: Table 2 summarizes estimates from 18 studies from 5 different countries, of which 11 estimates are from the U.S. The duration elasticities vary from 0.1 to 2, with a median of 0.53.
For the U.S. alone, the median is 0.38, and the range is from 0.1 and 1.2 in the US,
these estimates are imperfect proxies for the actual disincentive effects.
context: NBER Working Paper 22564, published in the Annual Review of Economics 2016 (peer reviewed); the quotations are read from the working-paper PDF, so check page wording against the journal version. Review by two academic labor economists of recent studies using administrative data and kinks in benefit schedules; no advocacy funder. Main limit: elasticities are for UI receipt or nonemployment spells in normal and recession times, not for the pandemic supplements, and the authors say they overstate or understate the social cost depending on the model.

statement: In the same review, studies of potential benefit duration in Europe had a median marginal effect of 0.13, meaning that one more month of UI raises nonemployment by about 4 days, and a median duration elasticity of 0.37.
anchor: The median of the estimated marginal effects is 0.13, implying that for a one-month increase in UI durations, nonemployment durations rise by about 4 days.
The median elasticity is 0.37
locator: Section on potential-duration effects (Table 1, Panel A)
context: NBER Working Paper 22564 / Annual Review of Economics 2016, peer reviewed; European studies of extensions in maximum benefit duration, not U.S. policy. Effects vary by country and economic conditions, and the review stresses these are measures of labor-supply response, not of total welfare cost.

statement: Ganong, Greig, Noel, Sullivan and Vavra found, using bank-account data on unemployed workers, that the pandemic supplements of $300 to $600 a week had large effects on spending but small effects on job finding, with implied duration elasticities of 0.06 to 0.11 for the $600 supplement and 0.10 to 0.22 for the $300 supplement.
anchor: Overall, we find that this increase had large effects on spending but small effects on job-finding.
The implied duration elasticity of the $600 supplements is 0.06-0.11 while for the $300 supplements it is 0.10-0.22.
context: NBER Working Paper 30315 (2022), published in the American Economic Review 114(9), September 2024 (peer reviewed). Authors are academics and JPMorgan Chase Institute researchers; the data are Chase customers, which are not nationally representative, and two designs (interrupted time series and dose-response difference-in-differences) give similar results. Workers' job finding was already depressed in the pandemic, which the authors note limits how far the results carry to normal labor markets.

statement: Coombs and coauthors, comparing states that ended expanded pandemic UI in June 2021 with states that kept it, found that UI receipt fell 36.3 percentage points while employment rose only 6.8 points by early September, with cumulative benefits down $2,529 and cumulative earnings up only $292.
anchor: withdrawal of expanded pandemic unemployment benefits in June 2021
Comparing the difference-in-differences between states withdrawing and retaining expanded UI, we find that UI receipt falls 36.3 p.p., while employment rises by only 6.8 p.p. by early September.
Average cumulative UI benefits fall by $2,529, while average cumulative earnings increase by only $292.
context: American Economic Association, AEA Papers and Proceedings, May 2022 (short peer-reviewed proceedings paper). Academic authors (Columbia, Harvard, Toronto, UMass Amherst); bank data from the Earnin app, whose users are low-income and credit constrained, so effects may overstate those for all claimants. The authors' earlier brief ties most of the job gain to benefits ending outright rather than to the lower amount.

statement: Ganong and Noel, using bank data, found that monthly nondurable spending drops 6 percent at the start of unemployment and 12 percent when UI benefits are exhausted, and concluded that the consumption-smoothing gains from extending UI benefits are four times larger than from raising benefit levels.
anchor: Monthly spending drops by 6 percent at the start of unemployment, falls by less than one percent per month while receiving UI, and then drops by 12 percent at UI benefit exhaustion.
consumption-smoothing gains from extending UI benefits are four times larger than from raising UI benefit levels
context: American Economic Review 109(7), July 2019 (peer reviewed); quotations read from the authors' working-paper copy hosted by the University of Chicago HCEO series. JPMorgan Chase Institute de-identified bank data for Chase account holders; spending outside Chase accounts is not observed, and the welfare conclusion rests on a model of present-biased households, which the authors present as one reading of the data.

statement: Ganong and Noel report that Gruber (1997) found food spending falls by 6.8 percent at unemployment, and that their own bank data show spending falling 6.4 percent on all nondurables and 6.2 percent on food, in line with the survey-based benchmark.
anchor: Gruber (1997) reports that food spending falls by 6.8 percent.
we find that spending drops by 6.4 percent on all nondurables and 6.2 percent on food
context: Secondary report of Gruber's American Economic Review 1997 result (PSID survey data, 1968-1987), read through Ganong and Noel (AER 2019, peer reviewed). Gruber's own NBER abstract (WP 4750) is not catalogued here; it estimates that a 10 percentage point rise in the replacement rate shrinks the consumption fall by 2.7 percent. The measure is food spending, a narrow proxy for consumption.

statement: Hagedorn, Karahan, Manovskii and Mitman, comparing counties on state borders, found that extending benefits from the usual 26 weeks to as long as 99 weeks raised equilibrium wages, cut vacancy creation and raised unemployment, and estimated that unemployment in 2011 would have been 2 percentage points lower without the extensions.
anchor: benefit duration rising from the usual 26 weeks to as long as 99 weeks
we find that benefit extensions raise equilibrium wages and lead to a sharp contraction in vacancy creation, employment, and a rise in unemployment.
unemployment in 2011 would have been 2 percentage points lower had benefits not been extended
context: NBER Working Paper 19499 (October 2013 version read here; a revised version later appeared as a journal and NBER paper). Academic authors; border-county design with an interactive-effects model and an assumption of perfect foresight about future benefits, which the authors say drives the size. Not the same as the Chodorow-Reich, Coglianese and Karabarbounis measurement-error estimate, which finds at most 0.3 point; the two disagree by a factor of about six, and the dossier presents both.

statement: Chodorow-Reich, Coglianese and Karabarbounis, using only the variation in benefit duration that came from measurement error in real-time unemployment data, found that benefit extensions had a limited influence on state macroeconomic outcomes and raised the unemployment rate by at most 0.3 percentage point in the Great Recession.
anchor: we find that benefit extensions have a limited influence on state-level macroeconomic outcomes.
increased the unemployment rate by at most 0.3 percentage point.
context: Quarterly Journal of Economics 134(1), February 2019 (peer reviewed). Authors at Harvard, the Federal Reserve Board and the University of Minnesota/Minneapolis Fed; identification relies on revisions to state unemployment data, and the Federal Reserve authors state their own views, not the Board's. Directly contests the border-county estimate of Hagedorn and coauthors.

statement: In DOL's evaluation of the recovery act, the Labor Department offered states $7 billion in incentives for UI modernization; 41 of the 53 UI jurisdictions already had or newly adopted an ARRA-conforming alternative base period and 36 had two of the four other modernization provisions.
anchor: (DOL) offered financial incentives of $7 billion to states to implement the modernization provisions.
for each of the 53 UI jurisdictions.
TUR trigger for EB. In addition, 41 jurisdictions already had or newly adopted an ARRA-conforming
ABP and 36 already had or newly adopted two of the four other modernization provisions.
context: Final report of Mathematica Policy Research and the Urban Institute for the Labor Department's Chief Evaluation Office, March 2, 2016 (Obama administration); counts of state decisions are from a 96 percent response survey and public sources. The report says the authors' views are not DOL's.

statement: The same evaluation's simulations suggested the recovery-act modernization provisions might have raised regular UI first payments by about 6 to 10 percent in 2012, but the authors could not reject the hypothesis that the provisions had no effect.
anchor: payments by about 6 to 10 percent in 2012. However, we caution that there is considerable uncertainty
about this finding given limitations in the analysis, and we could not reject the hypothesis that there
locator: Executive summary, final paragraph before the findings
context: Mathematica/Urban Institute simulation for DOL's Chief Evaluation Office, 2016, not peer reviewed; a simulation with admitted uncertainty, in a period when the recession and other federal changes overwhelmed any small effect. A later peer-reviewed difference-in-differences paper (Chang and Hodges, Social Service Review, 2024) reports that adopting an alternative base period raised UI receipt by 4.7 percentage points; it is not catalogued here.

statement: GAO estimated that fraud in UI programs during the COVID-19 pandemic was likely between $100 billion and $135 billion, about 11 percent to 15 percent of benefits paid; the Labor Department said the estimate was likely overstated, and GAO disagreed.
anchor: GAO estimates that the amount of fraud in unemployment insurance (UI) programs during the COVID-19 pandemic was likely between $100 billion and $135 billion. This is about 11 percent and 15 percent, respectively, of the total amount of UI benefits paid during the pandemic.

context: U.S. Government Accountability Office, nonpartisan legislative-branch auditor, September 12, 2023. Statistical sampling and imputation over 53 states, with a 95 percent confidence interval; the report says the full extent of fraud will likely never be known. DOL (Biden administration) disputed the method. GAO blocks downloads, so the words are read from the GAO product page through an Exa extract, 2026-11-16.

statement: The Labor Department's Inspector General said the federal government distributed more than $888 billion in UI benefits in the pandemic and that at least $191 billion may have been improperly paid, including more than $76 billion stolen by fraudsters.
anchor: During the COVID-19 pandemic, the federal government distributed more than $888 billion in unemployment insurance benefits. The Office of Inspector General (OIG) previously estimated at least $191 billion may have been improperly paid, including more than $76 billion stolen by fraudsters.
context: DOL Office of Inspector General press release of March 5, 2026, on testimony to a House Ways and Means subcommittee, under Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito, second Trump administration. The OIG figure applies an improper-payment rate to total spending, so it includes errors that are not fraud; the fraud figure applies a rate from DOL's program-year 2021 estimate. Lower and differently defined than the GAO range.

statement: Manoli, Michaelides and Patel followed Nevada's randomized 2009 reemployment and eligibility assessment trial for eight years of tax records and found that it increased employment and earnings and reduced short-term UI receipt, while about 40 percent of the sample was estimated to have negative effects on long-term employment, matched by increased entry into disability insurance.
anchor: Over the eight-year follow-up period, the program increased participants’ employment and earnings, reduced short-term UI receipt, reduced loss of homeownership, and increased Federal tax filing and tax receipts.

roughly 40 percent of the sample is estimated to have negative treatment effects on long-term employment which are corroborated by accompanying positive treatment effects on entry into disability insurance.
an experimental job-search assistance program that operated in Nevada from July through December 2009
context: NBER Working Paper 24422, March 2018 (a working paper; randomized trial, with administrative and IRS tax data). Academic authors, one at Treasury when the work was done; data from a DOL-funded IMPAQ evaluation; funded in part by Arnold Ventures. The heterogeneous-effects result rests on a statistical model of individual effects, not on observed subgroups, and many outcomes were tested without adjustment for multiple tests (per DOL's CLEAR review).

statement: Giupponi and Landais, using Italian social security data and quasi-experimental variation in short-time work rules during the Great Recession, found that short-time work sharply cut hours but raised headcount employment, that its insurance value vanished for low-productivity firms, and that it reduced employment growth in untreated firms.
anchor: Our results show large and significant negative effects of STW treatment on hours, but large and positive effects on headcount employment.
the long run effects of STW were null for the low productivity firms
STW significantly decreases employment growth and inflow rates in non-treated firms, and has a significant negative impact on TFP growth in the labour market.
context: Review of Economic Studies 90(4), 2023 (peer reviewed). Academic authors at Bocconi and LSE; Italy's Cassa Integrazione Guadagni Straordinaria, a program with an employer-size threshold used as a regression discontinuity. Italy had a double-dip recession, so the reallocation findings concern a persistent shock; the authors say short-time work is desirable for temporary shocks. German and French evidence on the other side is not catalogued here (see notes).

The state's business site and law-firm summaries give April 10, 2023 as the effective date of the amendments; that date is not in the saved text. statement: The Labor Department's national randomized evaluation of the WIA Adult and Dislocated Worker programs in 28 local areas found that intensive services raised earnings by $3,300 to $7,100 per customer (7 to 20 percent) over the 30-month follow-up and were cost-effective for customers, taxpayers and society.
anchor: Providing intensive services increased earnings over the follow-up period by $3,300 to $7,100 (7 to 20 percent) per customer depending on the data source.
this evaluation of 28 randomly selected local workforce investment areas
providing intensive services is cost-effective from the perspectives of customers, taxpayers, and society as a whole
30-Month Impact Findings on the WIA Adult and Dislocated Worker Programs
context: Mathematica Policy Research for DOL's Employment and Training Administration, May 30, 2017 (first Trump administration release; evaluation commissioned in 2008). Experimental design with more than 34,000 job seekers assigned at random. Follow-up covers the 30 months after enrollment in a weak labor market; the report says findings might differ in a stronger economy or with more funding.

statement: The same evaluation found, though not conclusively, that WIA-funded training did not have positive impacts in the 30 months after enrollment, because training was offered to only a minority of customers and many others got funding elsewhere.
anchor: Though not conclusive, the evidence suggests that training funded by the Adult and Dislocated Worker programs does not have positive impacts in the 30 months after study enrollment.

the Adult and Dislocated Worker programs offered funding for training to only a minority of their customers and many study participants who were not offered training from the Adult and Dislocated Worker programs received funding from other sources.
context: Mathematica for DOL (2017). The evaluators call the training result inconclusive: differences in training enrollment between groups were small and disappeared by the second year. It conflicts with randomized evaluations of sector-focused training in the secure floor register (EV-SEC-143), which find gains, and with Registered Apprenticeship estimates (EV-SEC-144); the dossier presents both.

statement: England's National Audit Office reported that apprenticeship starts were 375,800 in 2017/18, 26 percent below the 509,400 in 2015/16, after a levy of 0.5 percent of pay bills began in 2017, and that levy-paying employers used 9 percent of available funds in 2017-18.
anchor: The number of starts in 2017/18 was 375,800, 26% lower than the 509,400 starts in 2015/16.
a levy scheme whereby larger employers pay 0.5% of their annual pay bill
levy-paying employers used 9% of the funds available to them to support new apprenticeships
context: UK National Audit Office, nonpartisan auditor of government spending, press release of March 6, 2019 on a Department for Education program; counts come from the Department's published data. The levy and the UK program differ from U.S. Registered Apprenticeship; use as a design failure case, not a forecast.

statement: The National Audit Office wrote that the levy changed the pattern of apprenticeship starts, which fell after a spike before it took effect and had not recovered to previous levels, and that some of the fall may reflect a move away from apprenticeships that did not meet quality requirements.
anchor: the number of starts fell after this and has not recovered to previous levels.

Some of this change may be explained as indicating a move away from apprenticeships that do not meet quality requirements such as apprentices spending at least 20% of their time doing off-the-job training.
context: UK National Audit Office (2019), a government audit body; its causal reading is a hedged suggestion, not an estimate. Commons Library briefings (not catalogued here) list other suggested causes: complexity, inflexibility of levy funds, the 10 percent employer co-payment for small firms and the off-the-job training rule.

statement: Kasy and Lehner evaluated a job guarantee for long-term unemployed residents of the Austrian town of Gramatneusiedl (2020 to 2024) using matched randomization and a synthetic control, and found positive effects on economic and non-economic well-being, a reduction in long-term unemployment, and no negative employment spillovers.
anchor: We evaluate a guaranteed job program in Austria in 2020-2024.
We find positive impacts on economic and non-economic wellbeing. At the municipality level, we find a reduction of long-term unemployment and no negative employment spillovers.
context: Working paper (authors' site), published in American Economic Journal: Economic Policy; academic authors who co-designed the pilot with the Austrian public employment service. A small voluntary pilot in one municipality, so spillover estimates may not carry to a national program; the synthetic control is pre-registered.

statement: The Austrian pilot enrolled 107 people over 3.5 years, with estimated program costs of 237 euros per participant per month against a rise in participant income of 102 euros.
anchor: In total, 107 people participated in MAGMA over the 3.5 year duration of the program.
We estimate program costs of 237 Euro per participant and month. Participant income increased by 102 Euro.
context: Same working paper as EV-WRK-389. The cost figure is the authors' estimate of net public cost; participants were paid the collectively bargained wage floor, and the income gain is relative to unemployment benefits. Costs in euros at Austrian wage levels do not convert directly to U.S. costs.

context: Early findings report (December 2004, updated April 2007) by Abt Associates, an independent contractor, for the federal agency that ran AmeriCorps; matched comparison of members against individuals interested in service but not enrolled, controlling for interest and demographics, not a randomized trial. Reports attitudes and short-term outcomes, not earnings; the agency's later eight-year report (not catalogued here) found longer-run civic effects.

statement: Graversen and van Ours found, in a Danish experiment where about half of workers who became unemployed from November 2005 to March 2006 were randomly assigned to a mandatory activation program, that the job finding rate in the treatment group was 30 percent higher, mainly through more intensive contact with the public employment service.
anchor: about half of the workers who became unemployed in the period from November 2005 to March 2006 were randomly assigned to the program while the other half was not.

the job finding rate in the treatment group is 30% higher than in the control group. This result is mainly driven by the more intensive contacts between the unemployed and the public employment service.
context: Journal of Public Economics 92(10-11), 2008 (peer reviewed); randomized trial in Denmark, a generous-UI, high-activation setting, so the result may not carry to a system with lower benefits and less activation capacity. The result is read from the EconPapers abstract, not the full paper; the authors attribute it to contact and monitoring rather than training.

statement: Neumark and Wascher found, in matched March CPS data, that minimum wage increases raise both the chance that poor families escape poverty and the chance that non-poor families fall into it, with the second larger but not significantly so, and concluded that the effects more closely resemble redistribution among low-income families.
anchor: minimum wages increase both the probability that poor families escape poverty and the probability that previously non-poor families fall into poverty

The estimated increase in the number of non-poor families that fall into poverty is larger than the estimated increase in the number of poor families that escape poverty, though this difference is not statistically significant.
more closely resemble income redistribution among low-income families than income redistribution from high- to low-income families
context: NBER working paper, published in Economic Inquiry (2002), peer reviewed. The authors are long-standing critics of large minimum wage increases. Data from the 1980s and 1990s, at much lower minimum-to-median ratios than today's bills; Dube's later work with longer panels and more controls finds poverty falls (EV-WRK-066). The older, contrasting view in the poverty debate.

statement: Brummund and Strain found that the immediate disemployment effect of a minimum wage increase in a state that indexes to inflation is around 3 times that of a nominal increase, concentrated in the first 14 quarters after indexing begins, though the finding does not hold in their most restrictive specification.
anchor: the immediate disemployment effect of an increase in the minimum wage in a state that indexes its minimum wages to inflation is around 3 times the magnitude of the disemployment effect associated with a nominal increase in the minimum wage
though it does not hold in our most restrictive specification
concentrated in the first 14 quarters after a state begins indexing
context: Journal of Human Resources (2020), peer reviewed; quoted from the accepted version's abstract (July 2018). The authors call it the first empirical study of indexing. Strain is at AEI, a right-of-center think tank. The result rests on few indexing states and is not robust to the most restrictive specification; it measures the effect of indexing on top of a level, not whether indexing avoids the erosion that a fixed floor suffers (EV-WRK-023). No study in the register finds that indexing has its own benefits.

statement: Hicks and LaFaive, for the Mackinac Center, estimated that a right-to-work law lifted personal income growth by 0.8 percentage points and population growth by 0.5 points over 1947-2011, with little impact in the early years.
anchor: the presence of a right-to-work law lifted personal income by 0.8 percentage points and population by 0.5 percentage points from 1947-2011, on average.
The early years showed little impact from right-to-work laws
context: Mackinac Center for Public Policy, a free-market think tank that campaigned for Michigan's 2012 right-to-work law; not peer reviewed. State-level growth regressions over 64 years; the design cannot separate the law from other differences between states (a Michigan State University summary names endogeneity). Wage-level studies with stronger designs find lower wages or no effect (EV-WRK-165, EV-WRK-166). Presented as the pro-right-to-work side.

statement: Feigenbaum, Hertel-Fernandez and Williamson, comparing counties on either side of state borders over 1980-2016, found that right-to-work laws reduce Democratic presidential vote shares by 3.5 percentage points and turnout by 2 points, and that fewer working-class candidates serve in legislatures afterward.
anchor: to estimate the effect of unions on politics and policy from 1980-2016

Comparing counties on either side of a state and right-to-work border to causally identify the effects of the state laws, we find that right-to-work laws reduce Democratic Presidential vote shares by 3.5 percentage points.
Turnout is also 2 percentage points lower in right-to-work counties after passage.
fewer working-class candidates serve in state legislatures and Congress
context: NBER working paper, later published in the Journal of Politics. Border-county design, 1980-2016. It measures unions' political role, not wages; it bears on why fair-share rules are contested politically. One author (Hertel-Fernandez) later served in the Biden Labor Department.

statement: The national randomized evaluation of Job Corps, on 15,400 treatment and control youths, found that participation raised educational attainment, reduced crime and raised earnings for several years after the program, but on tax data the earnings gains were not sustained except for the oldest participants.
anchor: a nationwide sample of 15,400 treatments and controls
program participation increases educational attainment, reduces criminal activity, and increases earnings for several postprogram years
Based on tax data, however, the earnings gains were not sustained except for the oldest participants.
context: American Economic Review, peer reviewed; the Labor Department's randomized evaluation (Mathematica), on youths applying in the mid-1990s. The program's current cost per enrollee is in the secure floor's register (EV-SEC-639). The authors call it the only federal training program shown to raise earnings for disadvantaged youths; the fade-out on tax data qualifies that.
